name: Bloom's Taxonomy
statement: Learning objectives climb from remembering facts to creating new work, in a ladder of thinking skills.
statementAccent: in a ladder of thinking skills
meaning: Bloom's taxonomy is a classification of educational learning objectives developed under the leadership of the American educational psychologist Benjamin Bloom with a committee of collaborators, published in 1956 as the Taxonomy of Educational Objectives. Its best-known part orders cognitive skills into a hierarchy from lower-order to higher-order thinking. In the original 1956 version, the six levels, from simplest to most complex, were knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, and evaluation. A widely used revision in 2001, led by Lorin Anderson and David Krathwohl, restated the levels as verbs and reordered the top, giving remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, and create, with create as the highest level. The taxonomy was intended to help educators define and organize learning goals, moving learners from simply recalling information toward analyzing, evaluating, and producing new work. Although the cognitive domain is what people usually mean by Bloom's taxonomy, the original project also described two other domains of learning, the affective, concerning attitudes and feelings, and the psychomotor, concerning physical skills. The taxonomy has become one of the most widely used frameworks in education for designing curricula, writing objectives, and building assessments.
mechanism: Bloom's taxonomy works by arranging the kinds of thinking involved in learning into ordered categories that educators can use to specify what a learner should be able to do. In the original cognitive scheme, the categories rise from knowledge, recalling facts, to comprehension, understanding their meaning; to application, using knowledge in new situations; to analysis, breaking material into parts and seeing relationships; to synthesis, combining parts into a new whole; and finally to evaluation, judging the value of material against criteria. The idea is that higher levels engage more complex cognitive processes and often build on the lower ones. Educators use the taxonomy to write learning objectives with action verbs matched to the intended level, such as list or define for knowledge, explain for comprehension, or design and create for the highest level, and to align teaching and assessment with those objectives so that tests measure the intended kind of thinking. The 2001 revision turned the noun categories into verbs to emphasize active cognitive processes, and swapped the top two so that creating, producing something new, sits above evaluating, judging; it also added a second dimension classifying the type of knowledge involved, from factual to metacognitive. The framework thus gives a shared language for describing and targeting levels of thinking.

examples.text: The 1956 taxonomy ordered cognitive skills as knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, and evaluation.
The revision restated the levels as verbs, remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, and create, with create at the top.
Teachers use action verbs matched to a level, such as define for recall or design for creation, to write learning objectives.

variants.name: The three domains
variants.text: The cognitive domain of thinking skills, plus the affective domain of attitudes and the psychomotor domain of physical skills.

variants.name: The 2001 revision
variants.text: The Anderson and Krathwohl update restating the levels as verbs and placing create above evaluate as the highest level.

whyItMatters: Bloom's taxonomy is one of the most widely used and influential frameworks in all of education, giving teachers, curriculum designers, and assessment writers a shared language for describing and targeting different levels of thinking. By classifying cognitive skills from the simple recall of facts up through understanding, applying, analyzing, evaluating, and creating, it helps educators move beyond teaching that merely asks students to memorize, and toward fostering higher-order thinking. The taxonomy is used to write clear learning objectives, to align instruction and testing so that assessments measure the intended kind of thinking, and to scaffold lessons that build from basic knowledge toward more demanding cognitive tasks. Its influence is enormous and global, appearing in teacher training, lesson planning, textbook design, and educational standards around the world, and the 2001 revision keeps it current by emphasizing active cognitive processes and adding a dimension for types of knowledge. Even though its strict hierarchy has been questioned, the taxonomy's core idea, that thinking comes in levels of increasing complexity that education should deliberately cultivate, remains foundational.

working.text: identify where a learning goal falls on the ladder, from remembering facts up to creating new work.
state objectives with action verbs suited to the intended level, aligning teaching and assessment to it.
design instruction that moves learners from lower-order recall toward higher-order analysis, evaluation, and creation.

limits: Bloom's taxonomy is useful but should not be treated as a rigid law of how thinking works. Its strict hierarchy is debated, since higher-order tasks do not always require mastery of every lower level, and real cognitive tasks often blend several categories at once, so the neat separation of levels can be artificial and oversimplified. The familiar pyramid diagram used to depict the taxonomy is a later popularization and was not part of Bloom's original 1956 presentation, so the pyramid should not be attributed to Bloom himself. The taxonomy classifies intended learning objectives and kinds of thinking; it is a planning and organizing tool rather than a validated scientific model of cognition.
misreadings: Bloom's taxonomy does not mean a learner must fully master each lower level before any higher-order thinking is possible; the strict hierarchy is debated, and real tasks blend levels. The pyramid so often used to depict it is a later popularization, not Bloom's own creation, so attributing the pyramid to him is mistaken. And it classifies intended objectives, not a proven model of how the brain thinks, so treating the levels as a strict prerequisite chain, the pyramid as original, or the taxonomy as a scientific theory of cognition, misreads a flexible framework for organizing learning goals.
origin: A classification of educational learning objectives developed under Benjamin Bloom with collaborators, published in 1956 and revised in 2001 by Anderson and Krathwohl, ordering cognitive skills from remembering to creating.
